```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(lab4ridge)
library(caret)
library(mlbench)

data("BostonHousing")
set.seed(12345)
```

## 1. Training and test data

```{r split}
train_idx <- createDataPartition(BostonHousing$medv, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- BostonHousing[train_idx, ]
test_data <- BostonHousing[-train_idx, ]
```

## 2. Linear regression and forward selection
```{r lm-models}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

lm_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data,
                method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

fwd_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data,
                 method = "leapForward",
                 tuneGrid = data.frame(nvmax = 1:13),
                 trControl = ctrl)

fwd_fit
summary(fwd_fit$finalModel)
```

Note that leapForward does not include the intercept-only model (0 covariates);
that model only predicts the mean of medv and would perform clearly worse than
all models above.

## 3. Performance on the training data

```{r train-performance}
postResample(predict(lm_fit, train_data), train_data$medv)
postResample(predict(fwd_fit, train_data), train_data$medv)
```

## 4. Ridge regression with caret

```{r ridge-model}
ridge_model <- list(
  type = "Regression",
  library = "lab4ridge",
  label = "Ridge regression (lab4ridge)",
  parameters = data.frame(parameter = "lambda", 
                          class = "numeric",
                          label = "Lambda"),
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    data.frame(lambda = seq(0, 10, length.out = len))
  },
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
    dat <- as.data.frame(x)
    dat$.outcome <- y
    ridgereg$new(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, lambda = param$lambda)
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, submodels = NULL) {
    modelFit$predict(as.data.frame(newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  sort = function(x) x[order(-x$lambda), , drop = FALSE]
)

```

## 5. Choosing lambda with 10-fold cross-validation

```{r ridge-cv}
lambda_grid <- data.frame(lambda = c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50))

ridge_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data,
                   method = ridge_model,
                   tuneGrid = lambda_grid, 
                   trControl = ctrl)
ridge_fit
plot(ridge_fit)
```

## 6. performance on the test data

```{r test-performance}
rbind(
  lm = postResample(predict(lm_fit, test_data), test_data$medv),
  forward = postResample(predict(fwd_fit, test_data), test_data$medv),
  ridge = postResample(predict(ridge_fit, test_data), test_data$medv)
)
```

## Concluding comments

All three models perform very similarly on the test data. Forward selection 
(11 covariates, dropping `indus` and `age`) obtained the lowest test RMSE 
(4.41), followed closely by ordinary linear regression (4.42) and ridge 
regression (4.46). With a test set of roughly 100 observations, these 
differences are small enough to be attributable to the particular train/test
split, so no model can be said to be clearly superior.

For ridge regression, 10-fold cross-validation selected lambda = 5, but the
cross-validated RMSE is almost flat for lambda between 0 and 10. This suggests 
that shrinkage gives little benefit for this dataset: with 407 training
observations and only 13 covariates, the least squares estimates are already
stable. Ridge regression would be expected to help more when the number of 
covariates is large relative to the number of observations, or when the 
covariates are strongly correlated.

The test RMSE of all models is lower than their cross-validated RMSE on the 
training data. This is likely due to variability in the single random split
rather than the models generalizing better than expected, and the 
cross-validated estimates should be considered the more reliable measure
of performance.
